newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmakers let firm keep currency paper contract.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmakers let firm keep currency paper contract.

text.p: A Massachusetts company will keep its lucrative contract to supply the paper for U.S. dollar bills, at least for now, under a deal worked out by lawmakers on Wednesday.

An emergency spending bill passed by the House last week opened up bidding for a multi-million-dollar contract to produce the paper for U.S. currency. The sole supplier for 117 years has been Crane and Co. of Dalton, Mass.
The firm has been protected by provisions requiring paper to be made in America by firms at least 90 percent U.S.-owned.

The House bill would have opened bidding to firms only 50 percent U.S.-owned. A Crown Vantage plant in New Jersey wanted to compete for the work in conjunction with a subsidiary of the British-based Thomas DeLaRue company.
That sparked a bitter regional battle that helped to temporarily delay action on the House floor.
Under pressure from Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Edward Kennedy, House and Senate negotiators working out a compromise version of the bill on Wednesday dropped the open bidding.
"Today's decision should close the book on this outrageous proposal once and for all," Kennedy said in a statement.
But lawmakers told the Treasury Department to delay the award of a new four-year paper contract, pending an offical audit to ensure that Crane was not getting a sweetheart deal.

The General Accounting Office will also examine the effect of competition on the paper industry. Arizona Republican Rep. Jim Kolbe complained that the price of passport paper had risen dramatically since competition was eliminated. Crane also supplies that paper.
Even if the GAO found that Crane and Co. was getting a special deal, the contract would go forward -- unless the Treasury Department decided to take action or Congress tried to pass a new bill.

"Sole source arrangements are not in the best interest of the country. We do not allow them in the defense industry and we should not allow them in an area so vital to our economic well-being as the currency paper industry," Kolbe said.
